text: The source is declared. Now it's time to write this project's first real model — the staging model. Lesson 2's plan named this file: one staging model, 1:1 with raw_customers, light cleanup only. That rule isn't different for this project; it's the exact same rule from the prerequisite dbt course, now written against data this project actually loaded.

Here's the real file: models, staging, jaffle_shop, stg underscore jaffle_shop double-underscore customers dot sql. A source CTE selecting from source, jaffle_shop, raw_customers. Then a renamed CTE: id becomes customer_id, first_name and last_name pass through unchanged. One final select from renamed. That's the whole model — one rename, no joins, no aggregation, no business logic.

Line up the columns and the whole lesson is visible at a glance. id becomes customer_id — the one real change, because id is ambiguous across a whole project while customer_id is unambiguous everywhere it shows up downstream. first_name and last_name pass through completely unchanged, because they were already clear, readable names.

And notice what's true on both sides: raw_customers is one row per customer, and stg_jaffle_shop__customers is still one row per customer. Same grain, same row count — that's the 1:1 rule in practice, not just a rule you memorize.

Build it with dbt run, select stg_jaffle_shop__customers — building just this one model. A successful run reports OK created for stg_jaffle_shop__customers. Then confirm it in Snowflake with a plain select star limit 10. You should see the exact same rows as raw_customers, just with id now showing up as customer_id.

With a clean, correctly-named staging model built, the project has real, trustworthy inputs to work with. Next lesson, we turn 'trustworthy' from Lesson 1 into something concrete and checkable — real dbt tests, not_null and unique, written against this exact customer_id column.
